newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper tumbles after speculative-led selloff.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper tumbles after speculative-led selloff.

text.p: A big drop in LME stocks to their lowest in six years failed to stave off a speculative-triggered rout which wiped five cents off COMEX copper by the close.

Speculative selling began late Monday, and by early Tuesday the market fell through key technical support, triggering further selling which was then fuelled by options traders who had to delta hedge their positions, brokers said.
The downward spiral took a short break when the LME stock report was released, which showed that inventory fell 13,475 tonnes to 132,350 tonnes. Selling resumed as COMEX opened.
"It's the technical features in the market right now that caused the five-cent selloff," said Fred Demler, minerals economist at E D and F Man International.
December COMEX settled 5.05 cents lower at 90.40 cents, traded 93.30 to 89.70 cents.
Several brokers on both sides of the Atlantic blamed Canadian scrap dealer Herbert Black for initiating the selloff.
But Black dismissed the suggestion, saying he was out of the market, and had covered his short position last week.
Volume on COMEX was heavy at an estimated 20,000 lots.

Some traders said it was unbelievable that copper prices could tumble so far when LME stocks have shrunk by more than 120,000 tonnes in the past two months, and there was no fresh bearish fundamental news to justify the rout.
However, Black and others said the metal leaving LME warehouses was not all being consumed, but was merely shunted to off-exchange depots.
"Come the weeks ahead, we will see all this stuff being redelivered to the exchanges and people will come to realise it was all just smoke and mirrors," Black said.

Demler noted that while LME stocks at Long Beach fell 2,275 tonnes on Tuesday, during the same reporting period COMEX stocks rose more than 3,000 short tons as some metal was transferred from one exchange warehouse to another.
Combined producer, consumer and exchange copper stocks were now equivalent to five weeks of global usage, the lowest for over a year, Demler said.
"The stocks to consumption ratio suggests that copper should be $1.20 to $1.30 per pound," Demler said.
Despite talk of metal being moved off exchange for whatever reason, some brokers said business was still good, especially in the United States, and that premiums could rise.
